{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"An online age-checking system is identity infrastructure when it becomes the gate between a person and ordinary life. A statute may call that gate a “narrow safety measure,” but labels don't constrain machinery. If you must repeatedly prove something about yourself before you can speak, read, shop, or gather, the proof system starts deciding who you are (and who gets to know it).

What happens when your child reaches a screen that demands proof of age? You may be offered a face scan, an identity document, a payment credential, or an attestation from some intermediary. Each option can be described as revealing only a yes-or-no answer. That may be true at the moment of disclosure, but the process still needs a way to examine evidence, bind it to you, remember enough to reject reuse, and answer challenges. The “age check” is the painted button; behind it sits an identity machine. I don't need to assume a villain to see the danger. A gatekeeper that works once will be tempting to reuse, because every new gate can point at the same credential instead of building its own. First it proves “over 18.” Then someone asks it to prove residence, school status, employment, or a clean account history (the next “small improvement”). The capability expands one checkbox at a time – and the person becomes the bundle of permissions attached to the box.

Think of it as a universal key cut for one nursery door. The key may solve a real problem there (parents aren't foolish for wanting safer rooms), but once the lock is fitted across the building, the key-maker can map every entrance. You no longer merely show that you may enter; you create a trail of doors attempted, doors opened, and doors refused. Even if each landlord promises restraint, the shared key has changed the architecture. That distinction matters because privacy isn't just secrecy. It's also the power to keep separate parts of your life from becoming one searchable dossier. Your teenager's reading doesn't need to be linkable to your household's purchases; your political discussion doesn't need the same identity handle as a game account (separation is a security feature, not a defect). Join enough “minimal” checks together, and minimal data can produce a damn comprehensive map.

I mean “can,” not “must.” An age rule could permit local proofs that expire, forbid tracking, prevent a verifier from learning which service asked, and give people several ways to qualify. Those constraints are useful – but only if the implementation makes them hard to evade and the law makes them costly to violate. A promise of data minimization can't carry that load by itself (especially when the easiest compliance path centralizes verification).

You can test any proposal by following the credential after the green checkmark appears. Who issued it, who can demand it tomorrow, what identifier persists, what happens when it fails, and how does a person appeal without supplying still more identity? If the answers require a durable account, a reusable token, or a central broker, then we're discussing a momentary check. We're discussing a passport layer for the network – regardless of the name its designers use. I call this infrastructure because it can outlive the excuse that introduced it. Once websites, app stores, schools, and families are organized around a proof (even a privacy-preserving one), removing that proof becomes expensive and disruptive. Today's exception becomes tomorrow's plumbing. I would rather judge the system by the dependencies it creates than by the language wrapped around its launch.

Parents and privacy advocates don't have to deny every safety goal. We can demand that proof remain specific, unlinkable, optional, and disposable after use; we can reject systems that turn access to speech into an identity checkpoint. If we build a gate to solve a narrow problem, we shouldn't act surprised when every institution wants a key. Safety isn't the name of the system. Power is.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
